strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine gap in the literature: min-max/max-min optimization for non-smooth submodular-concave objectives, both offline and online, distinct from prior work on convex-submodular (Adibi et al.) or integer submodular-submodular (Mualem et al.) min-max problems.

Rigorous and self-contained theoretical development: precise notions of saddle point, duality gap, and restricted gap are given; sufficient conditions for saddle-point existence (Propositions 2.10, 2.11) are carefully derived and illustrated with worked examples (Appendix B) including a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium interpretation when no pure saddle point exists.

The proposed zeroth-order extragradient algorithm (ZO-EG) is a natural and principled combination of Lovász-extension subgradients (for the combinatorial minimizer) and two-point Gaussian smoothing gradient estimators (for the continuous maximizer), and complexity/hyperparameter choices are made explicit for both offline O(nm^2 ε^-2) and online O(sqrt(N P̄_N)) regimes.

Extensive appendix material strengthens practical relevance: relaxation of the online query-budget assumption from 4 to 3 function calls per round (Appendix D), discussion of alternative finite-difference oracles, and additional numerical studies (clustering, sensitivity to attacker budget ρ) beyond the main text.

Numerical experiments span two distinct application domains (adversarial image segmentation and adversarial semi-supervised clustering) in both offline and online settings, and qualitatively confirm the predicted behavior (e.g., sharp threshold in ρ, tracking of moving optima).
weaknesses: The comparison against U-Net in Table 1 is not an apples-to-apples baseline: the U-Nets are trained on a very small, narrow synthetic dataset (3000 samples generated by rotating/translating a single base image) and are never trained or evaluated under adversarial perturbations, so the claim of 'adversarial robustness: yes vs no' is close to true by construction rather than a demonstrated advantage of the proposed method; the conclusion that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' trained networks is only weakly supported.

All empirical validation is on synthetic, low-resolution (50x50) toy data (basic shapes, noisy blobs, two-moons clustering); there is no evaluation on real images/datasets, which limits confidence in practical significance of the numerical claims.

The core theoretical guarantees presume existence of a saddle point for f (Definition 2.1/Theorem 3.2), which by Proposition 2.10 is not guaranteed in general and requires special structural conditions (Proposition 2.11, e.g., common vertex minimizer) that are neither verified nor discussed for the paper's own experimental cost functions (segmentation/clustering costs), leaving a gap between theory and the examples used to validate it.

The online-setting guarantees rely on strong operational assumptions (at least 3-4 fresh function evaluations available before each cost-function change, and a bound V on the change in Lovász-extension values between consecutive functions) that may not hold in many realistic streaming applications, and the impact of violating them is only sketched (Remark D.4, eq. 63) rather than rigorously analyzed in the main results.

No empirical or theoretical comparison against alternative solvers for the same submodular-concave min-max problem (e.g., subgradient-based primal-dual methods, other ZO min-max algorithms); the only baseline is an unrelated deep-learning pipeline for one specific application, so the tightness/practical benefit of the proposed rates relative to existing techniques for this problem class remains unclear.

The theoretical contribution, while carefully executed, is largely an adaptation of established tools (Lovász-extension subgradients from Hazan & Kale, Gaussian smoothing from Nesterov & Spokoiny, extragradient convergence analysis) to a new but structurally similar setting, so originality lies more in problem combination and careful bookkeeping than in fundamentally new analysis techniques.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: non-smooth, min-max/max-min optimization with submodular-concave structure in both offline and online settings, which the authors convincingly argue has not been studied before.

The theoretical development is comprehensive and internally consistent: careful definitions of saddle points and duality/restricted gaps, a clear reduction from the combinatorial problem to a convex-concave problem via the Lovász extension, and detailed convergence proofs (with explicit hyperparameter choices) for both the offline epsilon-saddle-point guarantee and the online dynamic duality-gap bound.

The paper is careful about the subtleties of existence of saddle points for submodular-concave functions (Propositions 2.10/2.11, counterexamples in Appendix B), which shows good mathematical rigor and honesty about limitations of the reduction.

Reasonable complexity analysis (O(nm^2/epsilon^2) offline sample complexity) and practical discussions (Remarks D.1-D.4) about relaxing assumptions (e.g., 3 vs 4 function queries per online step) show attention to implementation realism.

Numerical illustrations (image segmentation, two-moons clustering) are provided for both offline and online, convex-concave reduction, and robustness-vs-budget trade-offs, giving some empirical support to the theory.
weaknesses: The flagship empirical comparison (Table 1) pitting the proposed method against supervised/semi-supervised U-Nets is not a fair or convincing demonstration of significance: the U-Nets are trained on only 3000 samples generated from random rotations/shifts of a single base image, essentially the same synthetic distribution as the test video, which severely handicaps the baseline and makes the 'outperforms U-Net' claim overstated and not generalizable to real segmentation tasks.

No empirical comparison is made against the most directly relevant prior theoretical work on submodular min-max optimization (e.g., Adibi et al. 2022 convex-submodular min-max, Mualem et al. 2024 submodular min-max), despite these being discussed at length in the related work; this leaves the practical advantage of the proposed ZO-EG method over existing combinatorial min-max solvers untested.

All experiments are small-scale, fully synthetic (50x50 toy images, two-moons clustering with <=50 points); there is no evaluation on real-world datasets or larger/more complex instances, which limits confidence in the significance and scalability of the approach.

The core technical contribution is largely a recombination of existing tools (Lovász-extension subgradients from Hazan & Kale, Gaussian smoothing ZO oracle from Nesterov & Spokoiny, extragradient methods), applied to a new but fairly narrow structural setting (submodular-concave); the novelty is incremental rather than conceptual.

Existence of a saddle point for the original combinatorial problem is only guaranteed under restrictive, hard-to-verify conditions (vertex minimizer, common vertex minimizer, etc.), and the paper simply assumes a saddle point exists for the main theorems, which weakens the practical applicability of the guarantees.

The convergence guarantees are of the 'best iterate within the generated sequence' type (min over a window) rather than for the algorithm's actual output at termination, which is weaker than standard last-iterate or even average-iterate guarantees, and this distinction is not clearly flagged in the main text.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, pushing most proofs, examples, and even some baseline details into a long appendix; the main text could better motivate why practitioners should care about this specific combination of assumptions (submodular + concave) relative to more general classes.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential ethical implications of adversarially robust segmentation/clustering tools (e.g., dual-use concerns), despite the applications chosen (adversarial image segmentation) naturally inviting such discussion.
No code or data release is mentioned, and several hyperparameters (e.g., tk, step sizes) are tuned per experiment without a systematic sensitivity study, raising reproducibility concerns.

strengths: First study to address non-smooth min-max/max-min problems with submodular-concave structure in both offline and online settings, filling a genuine gap relative to prior work on convex-submodular (Adibi et al.) and integer submodular-submodular (Mualem et al.) min-max problems.

The algorithmic framework (extragradient + Lovász-extension subgradient for the combinatorial variable + Gaussian-smoothed ZO oracle for the continuous variable) is natural and well-motivated, and the paper provides full convergence proofs with explicit complexity (O(nm^2ε^{-2}) offline, O(√(N P̄_N)) online duality gap).

The paper is careful and honest about when saddle points for the original combinatorial-continuous problem (1) actually exist, providing Propositions 2.10/2.11 with precise sufficient conditions and illustrative counter/positive examples in Appendix B, rather than silently assuming away a fundamental difficulty.

Extensive supplementary material: proofs of all lemmas/theorems, discussion of relaxing the 4-query to 3-query online assumption (with the consequent extra O(NV) bias term), and several additional numerical examples (semi-supervised clustering, robustness-vs-budget curves) beyond the main text.

Numerical experiments on adversarial image segmentation and clustering illustrate the qualitative behavior predicted by theory (budget/robustness trade-off, tracking of a moving optimum in the online case) and provide an interesting practical angle (no pre-training, low memory, real-time) relative to U-Net baselines.
weaknesses: The central theorems (3.2, 3.6) presuppose existence of a saddle point for f, which Proposition 2.10 shows is not guaranteed in general; the paper does not verify that this assumption holds for the actual experimental objectives (segmentation/clustering costs), so the link between the proved guarantees and the reported empirical performance is not fully established.

The comparison with U-Net in Table 1 is not fully apples-to-apples: the supervised U-Net receives image-only input while Algorithm 1 and the semi-supervised U-Net receive seeds, and the 'Theoretical Guarantees: Yes/No' row is presented as a clear advantage without acknowledging that the guarantee is an expected duality-gap bound under idealized/assumed conditions (known Lipschitz constants, saddle-point existence) that are not verified in the experimental setting.

Theorems are stated with t_k=1 sample per iteration, yet the numerical experiments use t_k=10-20 and hand-tuned step sizes/µ rather than the theoretically prescribed schedules; no sensitivity analysis or justification is given for this theory-practice gap, and no plots verify the predicted O(1/√N) or O(√(NP̄_N)) rates empirically.

The technical contribution is largely a combination/adaptation of existing tools (Hazan & Kale's Lovász-extension subgradient for online/offline SFM, Nesterov-Spokoiny Gaussian smoothing, and the authors' own prior ZO-extragradient machinery for nonconvex-nonconcave min-max), so the originality is more incremental (new problem setting) than methodological.

All experiments are on synthetic data (synthetic noisy images, synthetic two-moons clustering, synthetic rotating video); there is no evaluation on real datasets, and no code/data release is mentioned, which limits confidence in generalizability and reproducibility.

The per-iteration complexity analysis (Remark 3.3) and the online query-budget assumption (at least 3-4 function evaluations between cost changes) impose practical constraints (e.g., frame rate vs. optimizer speed) that are asserted but not stress-tested against failure cases.

strengths: Novel problem setting: appears to be the first paper to jointly analyze non-smooth submodular-concave min-max/max-min problems in both offline and online regimes using zeroth-order methods, filling a clear gap between prior submodular-minimization-only and convex-submodular min-max literature (Adibi et al. 2022; Mualem et al. 2024).

The theoretical development is careful and complete: the paper builds the reduction from the original combinatorial min-max problem to a convex-concave Lovász-extension min-max problem (Lemma 2.7, Propositions 2.10-2.11), explicitly discusses when saddle points fail to exist (Example B.1) and gives sufficient conditions for existence, which is an honest and useful theoretical contribution rather than glossing over a subtlety.

Convergence guarantees are given with explicit constants and hyperparameter choices (Theorem 3.2 for offline O(nm^2 eps^-2) complexity, Theorem 3.6 for online O(sqrt(N(1+P_bar))) duality gap), and complexity/per-iteration cost is explicitly discussed (Remark 3.3).

Extensive appendix material: detailed proofs, additional worked examples (Appendix B, E), and thoughtful discussion of relaxing the 4-query assumption to 3 queries in the online setting (Appendix D), showing attention to practical implementability of the theory.

Numerical experiments span offline/online image segmentation and semi-supervised clustering, illustrating the robustness-accuracy tradeoff induced by the adversarial budget rho and demonstrating that the algorithm tracks a moving optimum in the online video setting.
weaknesses: The central applicability of the whole framework rests on assuming a saddle point exists for f (as stated after Prop. 2.11), yet the paper's own Example B.1 shows this assumption fails even for simple submodular-concave functions; the sufficient conditions in Prop. 2.11 (existence of a common vertex minimizer, etc.) are abstract and hard to verify a priori for real applications, leaving the practical scope of the guarantees unclear.

The comparison with U-Net in Section 4.2/Table 1 is not a fair like-for-like comparison: the supervised U-Net is given only the image (no seeds) while the proposed method and semi-supervised U-Net receive seed information; the U-Nets are trained/evaluated without any adversary while Algorithm 1 is evaluated under adversarial perturbation implicit in its own formulation, making the 'outperforms U-Net' claim in the abstract/conclusion overstated as a general finding rather than a narrow, favorably-designed synthetic comparison.

All numerical experiments are on small, synthetic problems (50x50 synthetic images, ~50-point 2D 'two moons' clustering); there is no evaluation on any real dataset or larger-scale problem, so the practical significance and scalability of the method are not demonstrated.

No comparison against alternative optimization baselines for the actual min-max problem (e.g., subgradient primal-dual methods of Nedic & Ozdaglar, or other ZO extragradient schemes cited in the intro) is provided; the only empirical baseline is a qualitatively different deep-learning pipeline, so the numerical section does not validate the proposed algorithm's advantages over competing optimization approaches for the same class of problems.

The online guarantee requires a known deterministic upper bound P_bar on the path length of the online saddle-point sequence to set the step size h2; in real online settings this quantity is generally unknown in advance, and the paper does not discuss how sensitive performance is to misspecification of P_bar or provide an adaptive/parameter-free variant.

The theoretical bounds depend on several problem constants (L0, L0y, M, Dz) that must be known to select hyperparameters (mu, h1, h2, N); no discussion is given on how these would be estimated in practice beyond the illustrative examples, limiting reproducibility of the stated theoretical guarantees on new problems.

The final output requires a randomized rounding step (sampling threshold tau) to obtain a discrete set from the continuous relaxation, yet the empirical results largely bypass this randomness (e.g., thresholding at 0.5 in Section E.2) without empirically validating the theoretical guarantee under the prescribed random rounding scheme.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely under-explored combinatorial optimization setting (non-smooth submodular-concave min-max/max-min problems) in both offline and online forms, extending the Lovász-extension/zeroth-order machinery that has been successful for submodular minimization to a min-max context.

The theoretical development is relatively complete: convexity-concavity of the Lovász extension is established (Lemma 2.7), an extragradient-style ZO algorithm is proposed, and offline (Theorem 3.2) and online (Theorem 3.6) convergence/duality-gap bounds are derived with explicit, reasonably standard proof techniques (projection non-expansiveness, auxiliary sequence tricks from Nemirovski et al.) and detailed appendix proofs.
The online dynamic-regret-style bound O(sqrt(N(1+P_N))) is consistent with known dynamic-regret results in online convex optimization, giving the result some external validity.

Several illustrative numerical examples (image segmentation, clustering) are provided with discussion of hyperparameter choices and qualitative behavior (e.g., phase transition with respect to adversarial budget ρ), which helps ground the abstract theory.
weaknesses: The central structural assumption—that a saddle point for f exists—is acknowledged in Proposition 2.10 to generally fail for submodular-concave functions, and the sufficient conditions given in Proposition 2.11 (common vertex minimizer, etc.) are restrictive and not verified for any of the numerical examples. This sidesteps precisely the hardness phenomenon highlighted by prior work (Adibi et al., 2022) for the related convex-submodular case, making the main theorems contingent on an assumption whose applicability in practice is unclear.

The flagship empirical comparison (Table 1, Section 4.2) pits the proposed method, which has direct oracle access to the true per-frame seeds and solves the exact adversarial objective at test time, against U-Nets trained once offline and evaluated without seeing seeds (supervised case) or without adversarial training. This is not an apples-to-apples comparison of 'optimization approach vs. learning approach'; the claimed 'adversarial robustness' advantage mainly reflects that the baselines were never exposed to or optimized for the adversarial setting, which could be viewed as an unfair/misleading framing of the comparison's conclusions.

All numerical validation is on small synthetic problems (50×50 images, ~50-point two-moons clustering), with no experiments probing how performance/complexity scales with the problem size n that explicitly appears in the offline complexity bound O(nm^2 ε^-2), despite the per-iteration cost discussion (Remark 3.3) trying to argue this dependence is benign.

The online setting requires a fairly strong timing assumption (at least 3-4 function evaluations available before each per-frame cost change) and an additional bounded-variation assumption (Eq. 63) to relax this, both of which constrain applicability to genuinely fast-changing environments; the impact of violating these (Remark D.4, extra O(NV) term) is only briefly discussed and not empirically explored.

No code or implementation details sufficient for exact reproduction are mentioned (e.g., no public repository reference), despite fairly intricate hyperparameter tuning (different h1,h2,µ,t_k per experiment) that appears sensitive and hand-tuned per example.

The paper offers limited critical engagement with closely related work (Adibi et al., 2022; Mualem et al., 2024): it states a direct comparison is 'not sensible' without deeper discussion of what specific gap in approximability/complexity results this paper fills relative to those works beyond the general claim of being 'the first' to consider this combination of non-smoothness, submodularity, and concavity.

strengths: Addresses a novel and underexplored problem: non-smooth min-max/max-min optimization with submodular-concave structure, in both offline and online regimes, filling a clear gap relative to prior work on convex-submodular (Adibi et al., 2022) and integer submodular min-max (Mualem et al., 2024).

Technically rigorous theoretical development: the paper carefully builds up the machinery (Lovász extension, subgradients, Gaussian smoothing, extragradient) and provides full proofs for convergence to an ε-saddle point in the offline case (Theorem 3.2) and an O(√(N(1+P̄N))) online duality gap bound (Theorem 3.6), including explicit hyperparameter choices and complexity analysis.

The paper is careful and honest about a subtle but important technical issue — that saddle points of submodular-concave functions need not exist in general — and provides conditions (Propositions 2.10, 2.11) and illustrative examples (Appendix B) clarifying when the relaxed Lovász-extension problem recovers solutions of the original combinatorial min-max problem.

Extensive appendices provide additional robustness checks, e.g., relaxing the four-query assumption to three queries in the online setting (Appendix D) and discussing alternative oracle constructions (central/backward differences), which strengthens confidence in the generality of the results.

The numerical experiments span multiple application domains (offline/online adversarial image segmentation, offline/online adversarial semi-supervised clustering) and qualitatively support the theory, showing the algorithm tracks changing optima and produces robust solutions under adversarial budgets.
The paper is transparent about a limitation regarding sensitivity to the rate of change of cost functions between online iterations and discusses this with supporting remarks (D.3, D.4).
weaknesses: The comparison with supervised/semi-supervised U-Net in Table 1 is questionable as a fair baseline: Algorithm 1 is a per-instance optimizer with access to a hand-specified similarity graph and the true adversarial structure/budget ρ, whereas the U-Nets are generic learned function approximators trained without any adversary and with a fixed small training distribution; comparing parameter counts and memory footprint of an optimization-variable vector to a neural network's weights is somewhat apples-to-oranges and the conclusion that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' U-Net needs more nuance.

All numerical validation is on synthetic, low-dimensional data (50×50 images, two-moons clustering with ~50 points); there is no real-world dataset or larger-scale experiment to assess practical scalability or the tightness of the O(nm^2 ε^-2) complexity in realistic regimes.

Given that the illustrative submodular cost functions used in experiments are standard graph-cut type objectives for which efficient exact combinatorial algorithms (e.g., max-flow/min-cut, convex optimization via graph cuts) exist, the practical motivation for using a generic ZO Lovász-extension subgradient approach for the inner submodular problem (rather than a specialized combinatorial min-max solver) is not strongly argued; the advantage of the proposed general-purpose ZO approach versus faster problem-specific baselines is not quantified.

The core technical ingredients (Lovász extension subgradients from Hazan & Kale, 2012; Gaussian smoothing ZO oracle from Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017; extragradient method for saddle points) are each well established; the main contribution is their combination and adaptation to the submodular-concave min-max setting, which, while non-trivial and useful, is somewhat incremental in terms of core algorithmic novelty.

No code release or explicit reproducibility artifact is mentioned, which, combined with many hyperparameters requiring careful tuning (step sizes, smoothing parameter µ, number of samples tk), may make independent reproduction of the numerical results difficult.

The restricted gap/duality gap bounds depend on several problem-dependent constants (L0, L0y, Dz, P̄) whose magnitudes are not empirically estimated or validated against the observed convergence behavior in the experiments, so the tightness of the theoretical rates is not empirically assessed.
